newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street's open hinges on CPI data.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street's open hinges on CPI data.

text.p: The direction of Wall Street stocks on Tuesday will depend on how the market interprets key economic data, including the May U.S. Consumer Price Index.

Analysts said the CPI data and housing starts, both due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, as well as industrial production, due at 0915 EDT/1315 GMT, will provide clues as to the strength of the economy and the chances of the Federal Reserve raising interest rates next month.
Analysts said the data could either carry the stock market to another high or dampen the recent bullish outlook.
"On the whole, the market is going to take its cue from the economic data today," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
"A lot will depend on the numbers," said Larry Wachtel, a market analyst at Prudential Securities.

Economists are predicting a CPI rise of 0.2 percent for May, after a 0.1 percent April rise. "Core" CPI, which excludes food and energy items, is expected to be up 0.2 percent, compared to a 0.3 percent rise in April.
Housing starts are seen as flat, with new starts occurring at an adjusted annual rate of 1.47 million in May, compared to 1.473 million in April.
May industrial production is seen rising 0.2 percent after being flat in April. Capacity utilization is forecast at 83.4 percent, unchanged from April.
Japan's Nikkei average closed lower, down 87.41 points, or 0.42 percent, at 20,593.66.
In London the FTSE 100 was down 44.7 points at 4700.4. U.S. stocks traded in London were firm in light trading as investors awaited the release of the CPI.
The dollar edged lower against the yen, trading at 113.00/10 yen. In Europe the dollar was trading at 1.7355/62 marks.

The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that the Russell small-cap indexes are about to undergo an overhaul, with younger and more technology-driven stocks replacing older members.

The New York Times said in its Market Place column that real estate investment trusts have started to own property outright, especially office buildings, and are now hot properties themselves among investors.
